Name: Hannah Mitchell
Badge: Teacher as Researcher | Sustaining Literacy Routines
Looking back on this inquiry cycle, what did you learn about your teaching and your students that you might not have noticed otherwise? How did engaging in this teacher-research process shape or shift your thinking about your classroom practice?:

I learned that my students are hardwired for freedom and discussion when it is not graded but the minute I say something is graded or I attach a rubric, there is some rigidity in their thinking. Rubrics and grades are a part of my job so I've got to rework some things to make this process work for everyone. It was meaningful to reflect on each part of the process. I took a "let 'er rip" attitude and didn't provide a ton of sentence starters or thinking frames that I usually provide. I saw good and bad come from that.

Think back to a moment during the lesson sequence that stands out. It could be a comment from a student, an unexpected challenge or success, a shift in engagement, or a moment when your own thinking changed. Describe what happened and why this moment feels meaningful to you now. What does it reveal:
I really liked the visual representation even though that was the hardest part for my students. I had some students have true a-ha moments and do some amazing things. I had some other students who really struggled (surprisingly enough, it was my strongest students who struggled with the visual representation). I think this reveals some truths about how students think and how abstract open-ended reflections have a place in the ELA classroom.
As you look over the drafts your students produced in this lesson sequence, what early patterns, surprises, or questions are emerging for you? What aspects of your students’ writing are you most curious to explore more deeply with colleagues during our April regroup? What, if any, questions do you h:
I don't have any questions but I'm going to really appreciate a thinking partner to consider why my students had such complex conversations, lots of thoughts in their notebooks, and then flat argument pieces.
